storm.summary_layperson: Showers and embedded thunderstorms are moving through the area right now, and the Sound isn't offering the cove any protection this afternoon.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No marine-layer or sea-breeze buffer today — the Sound (74.5°F) is actually running about 8°F warmer than the air, the opposite of the setup that stabilizes storms, so nothing weakens what radar shows.
storm.detail_html:
NWS OKX's afternoon forecast calls for a chance of rain showers with embedded thunderstorms as a diminishing convective complex tracks east of the Hudson into a more stable environment. Radar (KOKX, scanned 3:50 PM EDT) confirms that's happening now: a cluster of shower/storm cells sits within 1–3 miles of the cove, with the strongest cell reading 46 dBZ well inside a mile of the shoreline.

Instability is essentially zero (CAPE 0 J/kg) and the AFD notes a fairly strong capping inversion overhead, which is why this reads as embedded showers and gusty rain rather than a severe outbreak — the forecaster rates tonight's severe risk "very low."

Normally the Sound's cooler water builds a stabilizing marine layer that can choke storms approaching the cove. Not today: water is 74.5°F against 66.2°F air, a warm-water setup that provides zero stabilization, and the sea breeze isn't running either (only 5% of coastal stations show any southerly component). There's no local mitigation in play — whatever radar shows is what the cove gets.

The nearest cell still actively closing on the cove per the tracking model is a modest one, 4 miles north, closing slowly at under 9 kt. But several other cells are already inside a mile of the coastline moving fast (21–23 kt) — those are essentially on top of the area as this is published and likely already producing rain or gusts locally.

The AFD also flags a second, potentially more organized round of showers and thunderstorms developing overnight into early Thursday as a complex tracks in from the Great Lakes. That's beyond this run's forecast horizon (model data only reached ~7 PM), so the back half of tonight's window carries more uncertainty than the front half.

What would change the call: if the capping inversion erodes, the forecaster notes an isolated severe storm "cannot be ruled out," particularly later this evening.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 4 mi north, closing slowly at about 9 kt; with no marine-layer or sea-breeze buffer available it arrives at full strength.

wind.tactics_blurb: Light gradient wind (~5-8 kt) with no sea breeze in play — ESE flow leaves the east shore sheltered by Tod's Point, so favor the west/right side of the course for steadier pressure, and expect the direction to wander rather than hold.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today is a gradient-only, light-wind day — no sea breeze in the mix (light gradient wind, no sea breeze). The land-sea temperature signal that would normally build a thermal is inverted: Sound water (74.5°F) is running about 8°F warmer than the air (66.2°F), the opposite of the 5°F+ gap needed to build a sea breeze. Only 5% of coastal stations show any southerly component, confirming there's no thermal driver today.

The gradient wind itself is light: the mean across well-sited airport anemometers is 7.2 kt, under the 8 kt cutoff for the lightest gradient category. This is a light, showery, post-frontal pattern, and regimes like this often carry unstable direction — agreement across the western-LIS station cluster is just 0.44, well below the 0.7 mark that would indicate a settled flow.

RYC (ground truth for the cove) is reading ESE 112° right now at 9.2 kt, gusting to 10. HRRR's own forecast for the next couple hours actually swings toward NE/ENE before catching back up to ESE by 7 PM — a 60-70° divergence from what the cove is seeing live in the near term. Trusting the live cove observation for the first hour or two rather than the model.

With wind out of the E-ESE, Greenwich Point (Tod's Point) shelters the east side of the course — expect the lightest, shiftiest air on the east shore and steadier pressure on the west side. Favor the west/right side of the course.

There's no thermal to collapse at sunset since none was running, but light gradient regimes like this typically go more fully variable overnight as the boundary layer stabilizes after dark — expect the wind to ease further and wander more through the second half of the window. HRRR's own forecast data only reached about 7 PM this run, so the 8-10 PM read leans on a persistence-style trend estimate rather than fresh model output; treat the back half of the window as lower confidence.

5-8 kt is light-air/drifter territory for dinghies — good racing for light-air specialists, marginal for anything wanting to plane, and with the direction wandering, expect a patient, shifty race rather than a hiked-out one.

data_caveats: HRRR forecast hours beyond ~7 PM EDT (f05-f12) were unavailable from NOMADS at fetch time — 20:00-22:00 wind values are trend-based estimates, not fresh model output.
